title: Counting Windows, Counting Squares
focus: Final week of new material. Windows that count instead of check, and the DP hiding inside a matrix.

cards.title: Window with a Budget
patterns: Longest window with at most k changes
Window never shrinks below its best
cards.trigger: Longest run you could make uniform, or valid, by spending a limited budget of edits.
cards.recall: Write longest-repeating-character-replacement from memory. Then answer the subtle one: the standard solution never decreases the window size. Explain why that is correct and not a bug.
useWhen: Longest repeating character replacement
Max consecutive ones with k flips
Longest subarray after at most k deletions
Fruit into baskets, at most two distinct types
Any window with an allowance of violations
template: max_count = max(max_count, count[ch])   # most frequent char in the window
# window size - most frequent = how many we would have to replace
# Max consecutive ones III: same shape, count zeros instead
keyInsights: `max_count` is deliberately never decreased. A stale value only makes the window look more valid, and since we only ever record a larger best, it cannot produce a wrong maximum
Sliding by one instead of shrinking in a loop keeps the window at its historical best size, which is exactly what we want to beat
The validity test is `size - max_count <= k`, which reads as 'everything that is not the dominant character must be replaced'
cards.trap: 'Return the actual window, not just the length.' Now the stale max_count IS a bug, because you need the window to be genuinely valid at the moment you record it.

cards.title: Iterator Design
cards.trigger: Expose a flat sequence over a nested or lazy structure without materialising it.
cards.recall: Write the nested iterator from memory. Then answer the design question interviewers actually care about: why is the work done in `hasNext` rather than in `next`?
useWhen: Flatten a nested list iterator
BST iterator with O(h) space
Peeking iterator, zigzag iterator over two lists
Streaming an infinite or expensive source
Any 'do not build the whole thing' requirement
template: self.stack = list(reversed(nestedList))    # top of stack = next item
# unwrap until the top is a plain integer
return self.stack.pop().getInteger()       # hasNext guaranteed a plain int
# BST iterator, O(h) space: push the left spine, pop, then push the
# left spine of the popped node's right child.
keyInsights: `hasNext` must leave the structure in a state where `next` is trivially correct. That contract is the whole design
Reversing on push is what makes stack order match list order. Forget it and you iterate backwards
Empty nested lists exist, and they are why `hasNext` needs a while loop rather than an if
cards.trap: 'What is the space complexity?' O(depth), not O(n), because you unwrap lazily. If you flattened everything in the constructor, say so and say it is O(n).

cards.title: Counting Along Paths
patterns: Carry the running max or sum down
Prefix sums on a tree path
cards.trigger: Count nodes or paths satisfying a property relative to their ancestors.
cards.recall: Write count-good-nodes from memory. Then extend it out loud: how would you count paths summing to a target, at O(n), using an idea you already know from arrays?
useWhen: Count good nodes, nodes larger than every ancestor
Path sum III, count downward paths summing to a target
Sum of root-to-leaf numbers
Longest path with a property along it
Any question where a node's answer depends on its ancestry
template: # Carry the running maximum down the tree
return good + go(node.left, best) + go(node.right, best)
# Path sum III in O(n): prefix sums, on the path, with a counter map.
# Exactly the Day 4 trick, applied along a root-to-node path.
seen[running] -= 1          # BACKTRACK out of this path

problem.name: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree

keyInsights: The `seen[running] -= 1` on the way out is the tree version of un-choosing. Without it, sibling subtrees see each other's prefixes
Prefix-sum-plus-map moves from arrays to trees unchanged. Recognising that is worth more than either problem alone
Passing state down as an argument keeps the recursion pure and avoids a shared mutable that you have to reason about
cards.trap: 'The path can start and end anywhere, including going up and over.' That is a different problem, closer to max path sum, and prefix sums along a root path do not cover it.

cards.title: Maximal Square
patterns: Min of three neighbours plus one
cards.trigger: Largest square or rectangle of uniform cells in a binary matrix.
cards.recall: State what `dp[r][c]` means, then write the recurrence. Then answer: why is it the MINIMUM of three neighbours plus one, and what would `max` compute instead?
useWhen: Maximal square of ones
Count square submatrices with all ones
Largest plus sign, a four-direction variant
Maximal rectangle, which needs the histogram stack instead
Any largest-uniform-region-of-fixed-shape question
template: # dp[r][c] = side of the largest all-ones square whose BOTTOM-RIGHT corner is (r,c)
return best * best      # AREA, not side
# Count all square submatrices: sum every dp[r][c] instead of taking the max
keyInsights: A square of side k needs all three neighbouring squares to be at least k-1. The minimum is the binding constraint, so min is correct and max is meaningless
The answer is the area, so square the best side. Returning the side is the most common submission error here
Summing dp instead of maxing it counts every square, because dp[r][c] equals the number of squares ending at that corner
cards.trap: 'Maximal RECTANGLE, not square.' This recurrence does not extend. You build a running histogram per row and call largest-rectangle-in-histogram. Two different techniques.

cards.title: Topological Order Output
cards.trigger: Not just 'is there an order' but 'give me one', possibly a specific one.
cards.recall: Write course schedule II from memory. Then answer both extensions: how do you get the lexicographically smallest valid order, and how do you get the minimum number of parallel semesters?
useWhen: Course schedule II, build order, task ordering
Lexicographically smallest topological order
Minimum semesters or rounds to finish everything
Sequence reconstruction, is the order unique
Longest path in a DAG
template: q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
return order if len(order) == n else []
# Lexicographically smallest: swap the deque for a heap.
# Minimum parallel rounds: drain the queue level by level and count levels.
# Unique order: it is unique iff the queue never holds more than one node.

complexity.time: O(V + E), O(V log V + E) with a heap

keyInsights: Deque gives any valid order, heap gives the lexicographically smallest, and the rest of the algorithm is identical
Level draining gives the minimum number of parallel rounds, which is the DAG's longest-path length
The uniqueness test costs one extra line and answers a follow-up that catches most candidates
cards.trap: 'The input pairs are [course, prerequisite].' Reading them as [from, to] reverses every edge and produces a plausible, wrong order. Check the direction out loud.
